opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it is that with global health or farm animal welfare, there's a fairly clear picture of what "good" looks like, even when people disagree about priorities. If you're distributing bednets, the main question is whether it works and how cost-effective it is. You can run studies, look at the evidence, and update. People can argue, but they're arguing within a shared frame.

AI is different in a few ways. First, the uncertainty is enormous and it's not the kind you can resolve with a randomized controlled trial. We're talking about a technology that doesn't fully exist yet, with effects that could be anywhere from "a big deal, like the internet" to "the most important thing that's ever happened." When the range of plausible outcomes is that wide, people end up anchoring on very different worldviews, and those worldviews lead to very different recommendations.

Second, and maybe more important, the interventions themselves often look like they could backfire. In global health, it's rare that a well-meaning intervention makes things dramatically worse. In AI, almost everything you might do has a plausible story where it's harmful. If you work at an AI lab to make it safer, someone can argue you're accelerating a dangerous race. If you push for regulation, someone can argue you're entrenching incumbents or handing advantages to less careful actors. If you do safety research, someone can argue it's mostly capabilities research in disguise. So you get people who share the same basic concerns ending up on opposite sides, each thinking the other is making things worse. That's a recipe for polarization in a way that "should we fund deworming or cash transfers" just isn't.

Third, there's a lot of money, power, and status tied up in AI right now. That raises the stakes and makes people more suspicious of each other's motives. If someone at a lab says something optimistic, people wonder whether it's self-serving. If someone critical of labs says something alarming, people wonder whether that's about getting attention or funding. That suspicion makes good-faith disagreement harder.

And finally, a lot of the questions are tied up with deep intuitions about the future, about technology, about human nature, about who should be trusted with power. Those aren't the kinds of things people change their minds on easily, and they map onto existing political and cultural divides in a way that makes the whole conversation feel more tribal.

So I don't think it's that people working on AI are more combative by temperament. It's that the structure of the problem, with high stakes, deep uncertainty, and interventions that can easily backfire, pushes people toward strong and opposing views.

r001.rationale: The response explains that differing views produce opposing recommendations about AI work—such as lab safety work, regulation, or safety research—and leave people on opposite sides, contributing to polarization.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, and I think there are a few things going on.

One is just that with global health, or even with farm animal welfare, the basic picture is pretty legible. You can look at a bednet distribution and say, here's roughly how much it costs, here's roughly how many lives it saves, and reasonable people can argue about the numbers but they're arguing within a shared frame. With AI, the whole thing rests on a picture of the future — how fast capabilities are going to move, what the systems are going to be like, whether there's some kind of discontinuity — and that picture is deeply uncertain. And when the core question is uncertain, people fill it in with their priors and their temperament, and then it starts to feel less like a disagreement about evidence and more like a disagreement about who you are.

The second thing is that AI touches a lot of other things people already care about. If you're worried about concentration of power, or about big tech, or about government overreach, or about the pace of economic change, AI becomes a kind of screen that all of that gets projected onto. So someone might say "I'm worried about AI" and someone else hears "you're trying to regulate my industry" or "you're a doomer" or whatever, and the actual object-level claim gets lost. With bednets, nobody's identity is really at stake.

And then the third thing, honestly, is that the stakes feel enormous and the timelines feel short to a lot of people, and that combination makes everyone a bit less charitable. If you think there's a real chance of catastrophe in the next decade or two, then someone who disagrees with you isn't just wrong, they're potentially dangerous. And if you think the whole concern is overblown, then the people pushing it look like they're trying to strangle something incredibly valuable in the crib. Both sides have a story where the other side is doing real harm, and that's a recipe for polarisation.

I'd also add that there's a lot of money and status around AI in a way that there just isn't around, say, cage-free egg campaigns. That changes the incentives for who speaks up and how. I don't think it's the main thing, but it doesn't help.

What I try to do about it personally is just be really explicit about what I'm uncertain about, and try to hold the view that most people in this space — on basically all sides — are acting in good faith and reasoning from different starting assumptions. I don't always succeed at that, but I think it's the right posture.

r001.rationale: The response points to uncertainty, regulation concerns, and opposing views about AI’s harms and value, but does not clearly attribute polarization to disagreement over which direction AI efforts should take.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it is that, with AI, you have to make consequential decisions on the basis of things we haven’t seen happen yet. With global health, there’s plenty of room for disagreement, but you can often point to a particular disease, a particular intervention, and evidence about how well it works. There’s a shared starting point.

With AI, people can have radically different pictures of what we’re even talking about. Is this a tool that will gradually improve productivity? Is it going to transform society? Could it pose a threat to humanity? And there isn’t an experiment you can run today that cleanly settles those disagreements. So people’s intuitions and ways of thinking about the future end up doing a lot of work.

Then the stakes make that harder. If you think AI could bring enormous benefits, slowing it down can look deeply harmful. If you think it could cause a catastrophe, moving quickly can look deeply irresponsible. The same action can look morally urgent to one person and reckless to another.

I don’t think that means we should shrug and say everyone has their own opinion. But it does mean we should be especially careful to distinguish ‘I think your forecast is wrong’ from ‘I think you’re a bad person.’

r001.rationale: The response links polarization to opposing views about whether AI development should move quickly or be slowed, with each side seeing the other course as harmful or irresponsible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it is that, with AI, people disagree about what’s happening at a very basic level. If you’re talking about malaria, there are disagreements about which interventions work best, but there’s a pretty shared understanding that malaria is bad and that preventing it is good. With AI, one person thinks we’re talking about a technology that could transform civilisation in the next decade, and another person thinks that whole picture is science fiction. So they’re not just disagreeing about what to do; they’re disagreeing about what conversation we should even be having.

And then even among people who expect very powerful AI, you can get opposite reactions. You can think, “This could cure diseases and make everyone much richer, so slowing it down would be terrible.” Or you can think, “We’re building something we may not be able to control, so racing ahead would be terrible.” Often those reactions come from taking the stakes seriously, but emphasising different parts of the picture.

There’s also much less ability to settle the disagreement with a straightforward empirical test. You can look at what happened after distributing bed nets. It’s much harder to test claims about systems that don’t exist yet, or about whether we’ll retain control when they do. That leaves more room for people’s intuitions and their trust or distrust of particular institutions to drive the discussion. And when the stakes seem enormous, that disagreement can become pretty emotionally charged.

r001.rationale: The response links polarization to opposing views about whether AI development should be slowed or advanced, describing these as reactions that drive disagreement.
